match.reason: The closest bank point, Types of data (mat-types-data-2), covers the whole idea but is written for Victorian Units 1 and 2 and adds nominal and ordinal material, which is a change of depth; mat-discrete-continuous-data covers only the numerical half, so a new point is the safer choice.

draft.title: Types of data
card: Categorical
data that names groups or qualities, such as eye colour, favourite sport or the street someone lives on.
Numerical
data that is a number and counts or measures something, such as shoe size, height or the number of pets.
Discrete
numerical data that is counted, so it takes separate values such as 0, 1, 2 and 3. The number of siblings is discrete.
Continuous
numerical data that is measured, so it can take any value in a range, such as 1.5 m or 1.57 m. Height and time are continuous.
draft.remember: Categorical names groups. Numerical is a count (discrete) or a measure (continuous).

a.q: Ava asks her class for their favourite pizza topping. What type of data is this?
opts: Categorical
Discrete numerical
Continuous numerical
Numerical
a.why: Each answer is a name, such as ham or cheese, that puts a student into a group. It is not a count or a measure, so it is categorical. Numerical is wrong because no number is recorded.
a.clue: Are the answers names or numbers?

b.q: Leo records how many goals each player scores in a netball season, and the time each player takes to run 100 m. Which pair of types is right?
opts: Goals are discrete, and time is continuous
Goals are continuous, and time is discrete
Goals are discrete, and time is categorical
Goals are categorical, and time is continuous
b.why: Goals are counted in whole numbers, so they are discrete. Time is measured and can take any value in a range, so it is continuous. Swapping the two is tempting, but a count cannot be 2.5 goals while a time can be 14.27 seconds.
b.clue: Is each one counted or measured?

b.best: Goals are discrete, and time is continuous

problems.detail: Shoe size is given as numerical data that 'counts or measures something', but it is a size label, neither a count nor a free measurement. It fits neither the card's discrete ('counted') nor continuous ('measured') definition, so it could confuse students. A clearer example, such as mass or the number of pets, would avoid this.
